01 / The challenge

A portfolio of products.
One operational story.

The brief asked Zebra to be positioned as an essential partner for defense manufacturing supply chains, with a message built around reliability, traceability, security, and compliance support.

The design challenge was to connect individual devices to a bigger idea: precision at every handoff.

01

The problem

Printers, scanners, mobile computers, and wearables can look like separate purchasing decisions. A feature-heavy presentation makes it harder to see how they fit into a complete manufacturing workflow.

02

The opportunity

Lead with the operational need: keep materials identifiable, information connected, and work traceable from receiving to shipping. Give each product a clear place in that journey.

03

The solution

A unified campaign identity and landing-page structure built around “Mission-Critical Precision.” Technical typography, signal-like accents, a product grid, and a connected workflow turn the offer into one visual story.

The strategic objective and campaign name come from the supplied creative brief. The design rationale on this page is proposed portfolio wording for review.

02 / Target audience

Built for the people
behind the operation.

The primary audience is decision-makers and influencers at Tier 1–3 defense contractors and manufacturers. The design needs to make the offer understandable across operational and technical roles.

03 / The central idea

Precision is
a connected system.

The campaign name carries urgency. The visual story gives it structure. Instead of introducing every device in isolation, the narrative follows the movement of materials through four recognizable stages.

Make the first handoff visible.

The brief introduces scanning at receiving to identify incoming materials and components. Starting the story here gives the audience a concrete entry point into traceability.

An engineered voice.
A readable explanation.

01 / Display

Give the message authority.

Squared forms and extended proportions echo technical interfaces and engineered objects. Large scale makes the campaign title the first thing a viewer understands.

02 / Body

Complex information.
Simple reading.

A restrained sans serif keeps product descriptions and strategy readable. IBM Plex Sans is shown here as a matching body-text specimen.

03 / Labels

Receiving / Production / Assembly

Compact monospace labels suggest identifiers and system information. The IBM Plex Mono specimen demonstrates this supporting type role.

06 / Art direction

Place the technology
inside the story.

The hero combines the campaign promise with a manufacturing scene and a foreground device cluster. It connects the product range to the environment in which the brief places it.

Context before specifications.

The facility setting introduces manufacturing immediately. The product cluster brings the message back to tangible devices rather than an abstract promise.

A shared visual temperature.

Cool blue lighting connects the image to the navy interface. Green accents link the scene, headline, and primary action into the same visual language.

Structure in the background.

A faint grid, thin rules, and precise alignment suggest tracking and coordination. They support the industrial theme without adding more copy.

07 / Product system

Different tools.
A consistent hierarchy.

The product portfolio uses a repeated structure: device image, family name, category, and short benefits. Consistency helps a busy reader move through a broad range without relearning the layout.

ZT / Industrial printersZD / Desktop printersZQ / Mobile printersDS / Barcode scannersMC / Mobile computersWearable computers

Repeat the comparison pattern.

Equal card widths and aligned type make the portfolio feel systematic. The audience can scan by category first, then read the details that matter to them.

Give the hardware room.

Isolated product images provide a calmer counterpoint to the detailed hero scene and make differences in device form easier to recognize.

Connect capability to context.

Brief benefit statements introduce a use case instead of leading with a long specification list. The workflow section then gives those use cases a sequence.

08 / The landing page

From the promise
to the next action.

The page moves from a broad campaign statement to specific hardware, then into a connected workflow. Each section answers a different question before the final call to action.

01

Start with the promise.

A dominant headline and a product-led scene create immediate recognition. The split composition gives the campaign message and hardware equal importance.

02

Establish relevance.

The supporting message and trust-related labels surface the brief’s priorities early. Their role is orientation; any compliance claim needs approved supporting language.

03

Make the range scannable.

A three-column grid introduces six hardware categories. Repeated image areas, title positions, and benefit lists reduce the effort of comparing them.

04

Show how it connects.

The left-to-right workflow mirrors the movement of materials: receiving, production, assembly, shipping. The numbered path changes the story from product collection to system.

05

Close with a clear action.

The final campaign statement brings the central message back into focus. Guide-download and demo actions give interested readers a practical next step.

Responsive direction: preserve the headline → image → action order on small screens, stack product cards, and turn the workflow into a vertical sequence. This is the proposed adaptation; the supplied campaign image shows a desktop layout.

09 / Motion direction

From a scan
to a signal.

Scanning and traceability provide a natural motion vocabulary. The examples in this review page explore that vocabulary; they are proposed treatments, not a reconstruction of verified original animation.

Illustrative labelPrecision in motion

A measured scanning pass.

A thin scanning line travels across an image or label. The movement comes directly from the campaign’s scanning motif and gives attention a defined path.

Reveal the workflow in order.

Highlight the active stage, then connect it to the next. Keep the sequence short and legible so the relationship between steps stays clear.

Keep content in control.

Use subtle border and color changes for interaction. Avoid moving essential text continuously. This review includes a pause control and respects reduced-motion preferences.

10 / Campaign extensions

One visual system.
Multiple touchpoints.

The creative brief also proposes LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram, and a product showcase film. These are planned campaign applications; the supplied finished evidence on this page is the landing-page artwork.

01 / LinkedIn

Lead with relevance.

Campaign launch, printer-family carousel, compliance messaging, wearable workflows, and a customer-story teaser. Carry over the headline style, disciplined grid, and product framing.

02 / Facebook & Instagram

Make the system visual.

Product spotlights, workforce stories, an in-action reel, and a vertical supply chain graphic. Adapt the content density to each format while preserving the green and blue signals.

03 / Product film

Follow the operation.

The brief’s 60-second structure moves from a manufacturing setting to individual devices, then shows the connected workflow and closes with the campaign statement.

11 / Design logic

Turning the brief
into a visual story.

This framework explains the relationship between the supplied brief and the visible design. It describes the design logic without inventing research sessions, testing, or a production timeline.

01 / Focus

Identify the shared need.

Use traceability to connect the brief’s audiences, hardware categories, and operational priorities.

02 / Hierarchy

Order the message.

Introduce the promise, explain the offer, connect it to a workflow, and make the next action visible.

03 / Identity

Build a common language.

Carry the technical character through typography, navy surfaces, signal colors, grids, and imagery.

04 / Application

Repeat with purpose.

Use consistent cards and section patterns so the system can extend across the page and proposed campaign formats.

12 / Design outcome

A clear story for
a complex portfolio.

The campaign artwork brings message, hardware range, and workflow into one consistent visual system. The design’s value is in making that relationship visible and giving the audience a clear path through it.

A recognizable campaign.

The headline, color hierarchy, and technical styling establish a consistent identity across the landing page.

A navigable product range.

Six hardware categories follow one comparison pattern, while the workflow explains their different roles.

A focused next step.

The page connects the campaign story to guide-download and demo pathways described in the brief.

Review notes

Ready to cross-check.

This standalone draft is built around the Mission-Critical Precision campaign you identified. Review the narrative and the details below before it becomes part of the portfolio.

Details to confirm before publication

Exact contribution and credits

Confirm your individual responsibilities for art direction, graphics, imagery, copy, Webflow implementation, and any produced motion. Add collaborator or partner credits where relevant.

Original font families

The screenshot shows the type treatment but does not establish the font names. Confirm the source families and adjust the proposed rationale to match your actual choices.

Product labels

The scanner card says “ZD Series,” while the brief specifies DS Series. The wearable is called “MT 5400” in the brief and workflow, but “WT 5400” in the product card. Verify the intended names in the final artwork.

Claims and actual results

Verify the artwork’s 40%, 60%, 99.9%, and 35% claims and its compliance language. The brief’s +25% traffic, 50+ demo requests, and 75+ sales-qualified leads are campaign goals, not confirmed outcomes.
